blocks.p: The address Rei had copied from the ledger's freshest knot did not go to a home. It went to a narrow building in Takinogawa with a shuttered noodle shop on the ground floor and a stairwell that hummed. It hummed faintly, the way a transformer hums, a pressure he felt in the fillings of his teeth before he could name it as sound. On the second landing someone had left a child's sandals paired neatly against the wall, the way the shoes of the dead are paired at a wake. The gift Rei kept folded down behind his breastbone opened one degree without his permission, the way a wound opens to weather.

By the third floor the hum had become something almost like chanting, except that no one was using their voice. It was the membrane itself being made to ring, struck and struck and held. Rei understood, with a cold drop in his gut, that he was standing at the back door of a room where people had learned to do on purpose what he had spent his whole life keeping accidental.

Through the gap of the door he saw them. Thirty people, maybe thirty-five, kneeling seiza on borrowed zabuton. They were not in rows. They were in a ring, and the ring did not face a shrine or a screen or a priest. It faced inward, toward a single woman at the centre in a grey summer kimono, hands loose in her lap, eyes closed. Every face in the circle was turned toward her the way sunflowers turn. It was not quite worship. It was the helpless geometry of things that have found their source of light.

The room was white. White walls, white paper on the windows, floor cushions and nothing else. Nothing else except one wall. That wall was covered from floor to ceiling in photographs of the missing. Snapshots, school portraits, a wedding print cut down to one face, a man on a fishing boat squinting into the sun. Some were laminated, the way posters are laminated when they are taped to station pillars in the rain. Rei knew that kind of photograph. Families had carried them up and down the coast in March 2011 and held them up to strangers. There were hundreds. Each one was somebody's unfinished grief, pinned where the ring could see it.

The air around the woman was doing something his eyes refused to show him cleanly. It shimmered like heat off asphalt, except the room was August-still and the shimmer was cold. Rei had walked into more haunted rooms than he could count. He had never walked into one that was this organised about it.

Then the woman at the centre spoke, without opening her eyes, without raising her voice. She said his brother's surname, which was his surname, into the ringing quiet. In a tone of perfect hospitality she added that the seat at the eastern edge of the circle had been kept open for some time now, that the tea was still warm, and that there was no need to keep standing in a doorway as though he were not expected. The congregation did not turn to look at him. That was the worst part. They did not need to. Whatever saw him was seeing through all of them at once, and it had been waiting, and it was pleased.
Rei took the eastern seat. Standing in the doorway would only prove he was afraid, and kneeling in the ring put him close enough to read.

He learned the shape of the room the way he learned the shape of a drowned man's last hour, not from anyone's account but from the body of the thing itself. These were not believers who had come for comfort and stayed for company. They were the bereaved of a city that had too many of them. A widow whose husband had gone into the 2011 water and was never properly seen home. A mother whose son's name was on a ward that no longer answered. And the man from Sumida, whose grief had been eating his sleep until something patient reached in and ate the grief instead. Each of them had carried a wound across the membrane, a thin place worn by loss. The circle did not heal those thin places. It harvested them.

The woman kneeling to his right leaned over while the ring breathed, as if they were old friends. She smelled of mothballs and menthol rub. "You're new," she whispered. "Don't worry. This is only a small one tonight."
"A small one?"
"Saturdays are the big circle." She patted his knee. "New grief arrives on Saturdays."
"How did you find it?" Rei asked.

"I didn't. Sensei found me." Her eyes were shining. "March. The memorial, on the anniversary. The fourth one, it was. There were so many people and I was at the back, I couldn't even see the stage. And a woman in grey came all the way through the crowd and took both my hands." She showed him, folding her own dry hands round his. "She said my husband's name. Before I'd said a word. How could she know that?" She let go. "Others came from the hospitals. Some from the little Tuesday circles at the community rooms. We call those the letting-go circles. Everyone is found somewhere."
She said it the way people describe being rescued.

A line surfaced in Rei's head from the chapter in Gin's book about cults, a chapter he had skimmed once, weeks ago, and taken for jargon. A cult, stripped to the frame, is a possessed person, plus a congregation, plus a spirit operation. He had pictured robes and chanting. Here it was in a white room above a noodle shop. The possessed person at the centre. The congregation kneeling round her. And underneath, the operation, which he could feel running the way an engine is felt through a floor.

Gin had written that the congregation has two tiers and that both must be read. Most of the ring were the first tier, ordinary people with no gift at all. They gave devotion, labour, money and cover. They were the numbers, and a standing pool to feed on, and at the worst houses, Gin had written, they were bodies that could be offered. Most would never learn what sat at the centre. They had been sold a divine presence and given the comfort of belonging, and for them that was enough.

But not all of them. Rei counted four who were different. They were mediums, the working tier, people who could touch the veil and run the rites. They sat a little straighter and their registers were open to the centre like taps. Across the ring a young woman in a school cardigan carried something inside her. It was folded in her like a letter in an envelope, quiet and settled. It had not been forced in. It had been placed there, and she had said yes. Gin's phrase for it came back exactly. Mutual-agreement possession. A spirit put into a willing medium to make her stronger in the service of the centre. She glowed with it. She was stronger than she had ever been in her life, and every bit of that strength pointed at the woman in grey.

Two places further round sat something worse. Two men, one of them in the reflective vest of a Grid courier. Their faces were present and still, and nobody was quite at home behind them. Something small and wrong looked out instead. Rei's register flinched off them. These had been mourners once. Grief by grief the circle had emptied them, and into the empty places it had poured lesser things, stray spirits, minor demons, small hungers that did what they were told. They were hollowed. They were vessels now. Rei looked at the courier's vest and wondered how many doors in the city it could walk through without anyone asking a question. Not a congregation, then. An army, built one grief at a time.

Thirty-five private erosions, gathered into one room and tuned to one frequency. The woman at the centre was the lens that focused them. And the relief on every face was real. It was the realest thing in the room, because to be relieved of grief is a mercy, and each of them had genuinely been shown mercy.

Rei made himself follow the current to where it went, because that was the only question that mattered and he already half knew the answer. The harvested thinness did not stay here. It was being drawn away, eastward and downward, toward the old flooded ground in Kita where he had felt the membrane scored on purpose, toward the held breath before the window breaks. The circle and the drained pool where Kaito preached were one operation with two mouths. Gin's ledger bound the grateful one careful favour at a time. Kaito's sermons tore at the wall from outside. And this room gathered the city's grief into a battery, and the thing in the woman drew it down. The horror was not that these people had been tricked. The horror was that they had been helped, and that their being helped was fuel.

The man from Sumida was three seats to his left. When Rei let his gift brush him, he felt the knot the ledger had described, the soothed grief, the leash of gratitude. Here in the circle it was doubled. The Healer's mercy and the Far-Shore's harvest had both passed through this man, and he no longer remembered a self from before either of them. He turned his head, mild and kind, and asked if Rei had also lost someone in the water. His face was so open and so unburdened that Rei understood the cruelty of what he was about to consider. To save this room, he might have to give grief back to people who would rather die than carry it again.

blocks.cap: The face that is two faces

blocks.p: When she finally opened her eyes, the congregation breathed out as one, a long soft release like a room of sleepers turning over. Several of them swayed where they knelt, suddenly tired, the way people are tired after being carried a long way and set gently down. She looked at Rei across the ring, and for one clean second she was only a woman. Close to forty. Kind around the mouth. A teacher's patience in the set of her shoulders, a few grey hairs left in on purpose. The kind of person who would remember a stranger's name and ask after his mother.

Rei felt the trap in that clarity even as it worked on him. The thing wearing her was letting him see the host on purpose, the way a card player shows one honest card to make the table trust the hand.

He knew the name. It was in the CVD copies Gin kept in a drawer at the flat. Fukai Rinka. A registered clairsentient, thirty-eight, gentle and good at her work, which was exactly how it had found her. Her file was old and the last line in it said alive. That was true of the body. Something had come for her in 2012, and it had not taken her the screaming way. A kishin is not a possessor that fights for the wheel. It is a resident. It moves in and puts the lights out one by one.

Rei reached under the teacher with his sight, the way he had reached into the man from Sumida, expecting to find two presences. In the man from Sumida there was a person and a leash. In Rinka there was only one thing. The woman was gone. They called her Kanna-sensei in the ring, the way people call a thing teacher when it has taught them to feel better. And under the teacher, patient and immense and not bothering to pretend otherwise, was the one the Grid filed under a single word like a held breath. Kishin.

At her throat on a cord hung a small grey river stone, smooth and plain, the kind a child pockets on a beach. Rei's sight touched it and expected an anchor, the grounding object a practitioner keeps to find the way back to themselves. It was not one. It hummed with Rinka's last true signal, warm and human and frightened. Anyone who read this woman would find the stone first. They would feel the gentle clairsentient still in there, and they would reach in to save her. It was bait. Rei pulled his sight back as if from a hot pan, and across the ring the kind mouth smiled very slightly, because it had felt him touch it.

Here Kishin did not bother with the sermon it preached through Kaito in the drained pool. It did not hide behind mercy the way the Healer hid. It simply let Rei feel its appetite as a fact of weather, like the cold coming up off a deep well. And the fact it wanted him to understand was this. It was older than the seat-holders' politics, older than the membrane plan, and it meant to sit above all of them. Every grief that arrived in this room fed it toward that crown. To Kishin, the Healer was a thief at the same harvest. And Rei, Yushiro's anchor, the one person walking toward Gin instead of away, was the most interesting thing to come up the humming stairs in months. He was grief that had not yet been spent.

She lifted the iron pot beside her, the one that had been keeping warm the whole time, and poured a second cup as though this conversation had been scheduled, as though Rei's name had been written in a book of hers the way the favours were written in his brother's. Drink the tea, she did not quite say. The kindness in it was real and the bill in it was real, and both being real at once was the whole nature of the thing. Somewhere east and down, the battery this room had spent the evening charging was waiting to be drawn on. The woman pouring his tea was the only person in Tokyo who knew by whom. She would tell him, warmly, for a price she had not yet named and he would not see until it had already been paid.
